The cyberpunk metropolis, known historically as Neo-Veridia, was not merely a city but a living, breathing organism of steel, glass, and data. Its origins traced back to the late 21st century, during the Great Resource Collapse, when traditional energy sources failed and corporations seized control of the remaining viable infrastructure. The skyscrapers that pierced the smog-choked sky were not built for beauty but for density; they were vertical slums and corporate fortresses stacked atop one another, connected by skybridges that hummed with the weight of millions of commuters. The neon glow that defined the nightscape was not just aesthetic but functional, a byproduct of the massive server farms and advertising algorithms that powered the city’s economy. These digital billboards, omnipresent and unblinking, did not just sell products; they sold identity, loyalty, and survival, their light reflecting off the wet, oil-slicked streets below where hovercars wove through traffic like blood cells in a vein.

The environmental context of Neo-Veridia was one of controlled decay. The air was thick with the scent of ozone, fried circuitry, and synthetic street food, a constant reminder of the city’s industrial heart. Rain was a frequent occurrence, acidic and warm, washing the grime from the buildings only to leave behind a sticky residue that caught the neon light in prismatic shards. The history of the city was written in the layers of its architecture: the lower levels, known as the Undercity, were built on the ruins of the old world, filled with forgotten infrastructure and black markets. Above them, the Mid-Levels housed the middle class and the gig economy workers, while the Spire, the highest point of the metropolis, was reserved for the corporate elite, shielded from the noise and grime below by layers of soundproofing and security drones.

In this world, where technology had advanced to the point of near-omniscience, the human element was both celebrated and exploited. The constant churn of humanity was not just a demographic fact but a resource, their data harvested and sold, their attention monetized. Yet, amidst this digital saturation, there were pockets of resistance and tradition. In the shadows of the alleyways, away from the gaze of the cameras, people sought solace in analog comforts.
